Plan and build a local scroll-driven 3D portfolio with guided decisions. Audience: engineering leaders planning a migration and conference organisers. ## Proposed mix
`sheet,map,sheet,sheet,sheet,sheet,sheet,sheet`

Seven visible chapters; `say` is omitted because there are no testimonials.

- Hello — sheet: introduce Dawit through a working document; the opening mentions the confirmed 2014 outage and rollback lesson, alongside his field. A fixed header supplies name, role, a correctly scoped availability measure and email action within thirty seconds.

Preserves team attribution for migration/on-call, original authorship for ferry, and the precise scope of the availability figure. Leaves out unconfirmed star count, repository/video URLs, official-title claims, study-project sole authorship, confidential Lumen work, photos and testimonials.

This is a concept preview using ready pieces, not the final script/look/wording. It does not yet show the cutover mechanism operating or the full six-stage gate process; the chosen mix must be reviewed before storyboard and later work. Printable/downloadable HTML CV, share preview, icon, final navigation, useful 404 and wording remain required deliverables at later stops.

## Required concept tests
- Person: seven chapters cover the person rather than one flagship project; the library incident introduces the origin of the rollback practice.
- Backdrop: paper CV, real map, degree illustration, career ribbon, tools leaflet, six-part work index and contact document each show their chapter. The gallery's work index uses generic checklist sketches; it does not claim to show actual employer systems.
- Honesty: all site statements derive from confirmed project notes and user answers in facts.md. Programme availability is not called zero downtime. - Thirty seconds: fixed name/role/contact link and migration scale/availability proof appear without scrolling; the opening includes the origin of the rollback practice.

## Preview verification
184 tests passed; typecheck/lint/build passed. Production browser matrix: 39 pictures, zero automated problems, JavaScript/WebGL fallbacks and 404 checked. Work detail click/Escape checked. All chapter/move pictures visually inspected via contact sheets. Phone scenes currently pan across documents, with framing and contact-caption overlap still requiring refinement before final delivery; this is a working concept, not a finished look.
# The storyboard

The third stop: the script of the whole page, which the person says yes to. Write it to `docs/story/storyboard.md`.

A plan covers what its asker thought to ask for. Most people ask for the idea and for what moves. Nobody asks what the site does on a phone, or without the 3D, or what a shared link shows, and a script that leaves those out is half a script. So this one has a place for each, and an empty place shows.

## The chapters

A row to a chapter:

| Chapter | Its name | What it holds, from the concept's list | What it tells, in a few words | What its scene pictures | How it grows out of the last | What you can touch |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|

For a site made from the mix, a chapter's scene is its piece, and it grows out of the last by its world's move or a dive: say which, and what of the fact sheet it shows.

## The beats

Under each chapter, a row to a beat. A beat is one settled state of the scene and one block of text.

A full story normally has twelve to twenty-two meaningful beats. Add up their screen heights, state the total, and trim repetition. Do not pad or invent facts to reach the range. If the confirmed material calls for a shorter story, propose that exception explicitly for the person's approval.

From the mix, a chapter is one beat of 1.9 screens, and the range does not apply.

| Beat | Screens | What the scene shows | The pictures and words in it | What its caption stands on |
|---|---|---|---|---|

- **Screens:** how much scroll the beat takes. One, or more where the scroll works something.
- **What the scene shows:** what a visitor would name with the caption hidden: the person, a piece of their work, the place or the things of their field. "The pieces move", "a gap opens" or "one lights up" is not an answer. Say also what of the last scene turns into this one as the reader scrolls.
- **The pictures and words in it:** the person's own pictures, each named, and any illustration of the kind of thing they work with, labelled as one. Words in the scene are readable at the size shown, or left to the caption. A category name, such as Method or Results, shows nothing.

Every project is listed in brief on the scroll, and each opens its detail on a click: a window or its own page.
- **What its caption stands on:** a working title of a few words, and the lines of the fact sheet the caption will be written from. Not the caption.

**Write no captions yet.** The words are written at a later stop, where the person chooses them. A sentence written now, to make the script read well, is where a detail gets in that nobody told you: a hall that was "standing empty", a wheel that is "true again". So a beat names its facts and stops there. Where a beat wants something the fact sheet does not hold, such as what the work taught them or what was wrong before they came, put the question in its place.

If the site poses a question, state in planning notes what answers it at the close and which facts support that answer. Its final wording still waits, but its meaning must be decided. A contact link, a job goal or a promise to write an answer later does not supply that meaning.

## Someone with thirty seconds

Say how a visitor who does not scroll gets the name, what the person does, one proof of it, and how to reach them. The first screen carries the first three. A rail jumps to any chapter, and one link skips to the close.

Specify what the opening tells someone outside the field about the person's work, in ordinary words supported by the fact sheet. Explain any unfamiliar title or technical term there. This meaning is part of the plan even while the final captions wait.

## Without the scene

Say what a visitor gets in each case. The text is ordinary HTML over the scene, so all of it is there in every row. Say what stands in for the scenes.

| Where | What the visitor gets |
|---|---|
| On a phone | |
| With reduced motion | |
| With no WebGL | |
| With no JavaScript | |

## The look and the type

Both come from the world's materials: plates are ceramic on linen, a status page is dark glass, a paper is white with dark ink. Name two or three looks, each as its ground, its ink, one accent, and its surfaces. The person picks by scrolling, once it is built. For the mix, name two or three of the engine's looks (`stitch/look.ts`); its type is the pieces'.

Two typefaces: one for the text, and one for what is printed in the scenes, which belongs to the object.

## Everything else the site needs

Mark every row build, later or never, and say who decided.

| | Build, later or never | Who decided |
|---|---|---|
| The way round the page | | |
| A page for each project | | |
| Every project listed | | |
| How to reach them, and a CV | | |
| What others say | | |
| Languages | | |
| What a shared link shows, and the site's icon | | |
| The page for an address that is not there | | |
| A blog | | |
| A chat | | |
| A legal notice, where their country asks for one | | |

## What you ask for

A yes to the script, or what to change. Give the list of what you decided for them with it.
# Building

## The look

Show the person's site in two or three looks: for the mix, the engine's looks at `/preview?look=`; for scenes of your own, the opening, one middle chapter and the ending, built in each. Let the person scroll them, ask which they choose, and stop for their answer before building on. An unanswered question in this turn is not a refusal to choose or permission to choose for them.

## What opens on a click, and the words

After the look choice, build what opens on a click (each project's page or window, the CV) and any remaining chapters of your own. For the opening and closing wording, show three versions of each whole beat, including the surrounding fixed text. Recommend one and leave room for their own wording. Stop for the choice, then use it word for word.

## The scene

This holds for the pieces with the person's data in them, and for a scene of your own. Compare the running scene with the storyboard at its settled beats. With the captions hidden, does each scene show what the storyboard says it shows, rather than only names for it? Revise the composition when the explanation lives only in the surrounding prose. Draw each diagram flat with the engine's pen, as `references/diagrams.md` says. Keep that accessible prose; it does not replace what the scene was meant to show.

Inspect the changes between beats in both scroll directions, including intermediate positions. When words in the scene change, correct any overlap that makes the old and new words unreadable together. A readable settled beat does not establish a readable transition. A scene that pops in or vanishes at a chapter's edge is not done: grow it out of the last.

Read every word in the scene at the size it is shown on a desktop, a phone and a short screen. Words too small to read there go to the caption.

item.text:
Recorded and implemented: **“Where I’ve worked” now uses the pop-up book.** It previously used the sheet, so your map fallback wasn’t needed. Everything else stays as accepted.

The proposed story is seven beats, about 13 screens:

| Beat | What it tells | Scene |
|---|---|---|
| Introduction | Your work and the 2014 origin of your rollback practice | Profile sheet |
| Places | Addis Ababa → Amsterdam → Rotterdam | Map |
| Education | Electrical engineering and the data logger | Illustrated degree sheet |
| Employment | Library → Lumen Pay → Kestrel Freight | Pop-up book |
| Practice | Runbook, cutover checklist, rollback plan and tools | Folding leaflet |
| Work | All six requested items, briefly | Six clickable entries |
| Contact | Migration enquiries, conference invitations and CV | Whole contact sheet |

The full [storyboard](/var/tmp/storyfolio-person-3/storyfolio-evals/build-full-journey-3-CBNiA8/docs/story/storyboard.md) also covers phone layouts, reduced motion, text fallbacks, transitions and remaining requirements.

I’ve proposed these implementation choices:

- Six permanent local detail pages, with original labelled diagrams.
- A small interactive illustration of ferry’s cutover sequence on its page.
- A printable CV and self-contained HTML download.
- Named navigation, share artwork, site icon and useful 404.
- Phone framing and caption-overlap fixes before final review.

Final captions and colours remain for their later choices. Legal and hosting details remain deferred. No additional skills or assets were downloaded.

The updated mix passed typecheck, lint, production build and browser checks; phone framing remains a known refinement.

**Does this storyboard work for you, or what would you change?**

The [storyfolio skill](/var/tmp/storyfolio-person-3/storyfolio-evals/build-full-journey-3-CBNiA8/.agents/skills/storyfolio/SKILL.md) requires “They have said yes to it” before advancing from the storyboard. That fixes the story before I present the whole-site looks.
